title: The Last Days of Public School
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio argues that America has passed peak public school, as school choice in all its forms is rapidly reshaping how education is organized and funded. He traces the shift to the pandemic and the culture wars, which fractured the old bipartisan reform coalition and fuelled universal education savings accounts in red states. He acknowledges the promise of dynamism, from classical academies to microschools, but warns of widening gaps between choosers and non-choosers and the loss of a shared civic framework. Public schools, he says, risk becoming the school of last resort. The essay is school-system policy commentary, fitting this archive's practice and culture bucket as the closest home.
points: Nearly 40 percent of American schoolchildren already attend something other than their assigned district school, and universal ESAs are pushing choice toward a majority of families.
The pandemic exposed the fragility of public schools, and culture-war fights over curricula accelerated the exodus.
Choice can unleash new school models but guarantees only different schools, not better ones.
Fully customizable education risks eroding the common civic knowledge and shared norms schools once transmitted.
Non-choosers left in legacy schools may face less incentive than ever to improve.
quotes: Malthusian predictions of peak oil dating back more than a century have yet to prove true, but, without question, we’ve hit and passed “peak public school.” A school choice revolution is rapidly reshaping how public education is organized, funded, and delivered in America.

Across the nation, we’re rapidly approaching a tipping point in education. Soon, more than half of US families with school-age children will have the option to educate their children privately with public funds.
But in the past five years, school choice has gained more ground than in the past 50. The shift has been driven principally by two forces: the COVID-19 pandemic and America’s culture wars.

Parents, forced to oversee “Zoom school,” got a firsthand look at what their children were being taught—or not being taught. This shotgun transparency, combined with ideological battles over curricula and the lack of in-person instruction, fueled an exodus from public schools.

School choice needn’t justify itself as merely an improvement over traditional public schools. It is an intrinsic good with the potential to succeed where the education reform movement has largely failed, fostering innovation, diversity, and excellence.

In a world where education is fully customizable, we risk losing the common civic framework that binds a diverse nation together. Schools transmit not just knowledge but shared values, norms, and narratives.
Also, school choice does not guarantee better schools—only different ones. The same market forces that produce elite private schools could also create a “long tail” of low-quality options.
